newsitem.title: USA: US labor mkt tight, NAIRU may be lower -- K.C. Fed.
newsitem.headline: US labor mkt tight, NAIRU may be lower -- K.C. Fed.

text.p: U.S. labor markets are tight, with the economy operating a bit beyond capacity but still without inflationary pressures, an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City said.

"Labor markets are clearly tight, and I've been somewhat surprised by the lack of price pressures to date given the strength of the labor markets," said Stuart Weiner, vice-president and an economist at the Kansas City Fed.

Weiner, who is an expert on the relationship between labor markets and inflation, said the current economic scenario has led him to lower his estimates for the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU) to somewhere closer to 5.5 percent than 6.0 percent.

"I've been surprised we haven't seen more price pressures than we have and it certainly led me to lower my estimate of the NAIRU, at least temporarily, to closer to 5.5 percent than to 6.0 percent," Weiner said.
The Kansas City Fed economist said, however, that the central bank cannot become complacent, adding that the NAIRU framework is still at work.
"We can't become complacent ... the dynamics are still at work and it's just a question of timing and magnitude," Weiner told Reuters in a telephone interview on Friday.

"The economy is operating a little bit beyond capacity and I would, consistent with that, say there is some modest increase in inflation potentially down the road," the Kansas City Fed economist added.
Weiner said the economy has performed well. But he warned that one has to be prudent in asserting the nation has entered a new economic era.

"I would be uncomfortable with an assertion that the U.S. economy can continue to operate at a 4.9-percent unemployment rate with growth above three percent without seeing inflationary presesures," Weiner said.
The Labor Department released its April employment report on Friday, which showed the unemployment rate dropped to 4.9 percent last month against 5.2 percent in March.
Weiner suggested some reasons why he believes the NAIRU has temporarily dropped and why inflation has remained in check despite the tightness in the labor markets.
Weiner said workers' insecurity about their jobs could be one of the factors. "Workers have been less demanding ... but it's probably a temporary phenomenon," Weiner said.
The Kansas City Fed economist added that productivity gains may have also helped lower the NAIRU.
"We ought to be seeing some improvement in productivity gains given the high level of investment in computers and other high-tech equipment.

"So perhaps productivity growth is rising but we're not measuring it properly ... that would serve to lower the natural rate at least until workers start to catch up and start to raise their wage demands," he added.
The Kansas City economist also said the strength of the U.S. dollar against other major currencies was a factor holding down inflation. However, that factor may also be temporary, he added.
"The appreciation of the dollar is something that may not be repeated," Weiner said.
